PA3605 Cosmology: additional material for Lecture 8

The cosmological constant

Einstein originally introduce the so-called cosmological constant as an extra term in his equations of general relativity, in order to permit static solutions (without it, as we’ve seen, the Universe either expands or contracts, but can’t be static). In the Newtonian limit this constant – which is denoted Λ – appears as an additional term in the Poisson equation, such that

∇2⁡Φ+Λ=4⁢π⁢G⁢ρ (1)

Einstein later referred to this as his “greatest blunder”, and for a long time it was regarded either a mistake, or as an irrelevant mathematical curiosity. However, the discovery that our Universe is accelerating re-ignited interest in the cosmological constant, and – as we will see – it’s now regarded as an integral part of modern cosmology.

To consider the effects of Λ, we can go back and re-derive the equations of cosmology with this extra term included. It appears as an additional, constant term everywhere, so the Friedmann equation becomes

H2=8⁢π⁢G3⁢ρ-k⁢c2a2+Λ3 (2)

The fluid equation is unchanged by the addition of a cosmological constant (as it has no gravitational terms), and we can re-derive a new acceleration equation from this revised Friedmann equation (following the same steps as in Lecture 3):

a¨a=-43⁢π⁢G⁢(ρ+3⁢pc2)+Λ3 (3)

Λ has dimensions of time-2 (though beware “natural units” and factors of c2 when looking at the literature here), and can in general take on both positive and negative values. However, in light of what we know about the acceleration of the Universe, solutions with positive Λ are the ones of most interest. We see from Equation 3 that a positive cosmological constant gives rise to a positive acceleration, essentially acting as a repulsive gravitational force. Moreover, if Λ is large enough it can overcome the attractive gravity of normal matter and give us an accelerating Universe.

Following on from Lecture 7, it’s also helpful to define a density parameter for Λ. We can do this trivially from Equation 2:

ΩΛ=Λ3⁢H2 (4)

Note that although Λ is a constant here, ΩΛ is not (because H varies with time). As before, we can then re-write the Friedmann equation in terms of the density parameter(s) to find

Ω+ΩΛ-1=k⁢c2H2⁢a2 (5)

Note that here Ω represents all the other contributions to the density; in the present-day Universe this basically just matter (radiation is largely negligible111 Measuring the present-day radiation density from the cosmic microwave background gives Ωr,0≃10-4.), so to a very good approximation Ω0≃Ωm. In the present-day Universe

Ωm+ΩΛ=1 (6)

is therefore the solution of a flat Universe, and the boundary between open (0<Ωm+ΩΛ<1) and closed (Ωm+ΩΛ>1) Universes. A key goal of cosmology is to work out where in the (Ωm, ΩΛ) plane the real Universe lies.

Fluid description of Λ

It is often useful to define the cosmological constant in terms of an energy density and pressure, which we denote ρΛ and pΛ, respectively. If we re-write Equation 2 as

H2=8⁢π⁢G3⁢(ρ+ρΛ)-k⁢c2a2 (7)

then we require

ρΛ=Λ8⁢π⁢G (8)

and we see that ΩΛ=ρΛ/ρc, as expected. If we consider this form of the Friedmann equation and seek to keep the acceleration equation in its standard form, then we require that pΛ=-ρΛ⁢c2. The cosmological constant therefore has a negative pressure: work is done on it (rather than by it) as its volume expands. Indeed this is required if the energy density associated with Λ is to remain constant as the Universe expands222 More generally, cosmologists often consider equations of state of the form pv=w⁢ρv⁢c2. Here w can take on any value, and Λ corresponds to the special case of (constant) w=-1. The most recent (2018) results from Planck find w=-1.03±0.03, so our Universe therefore is consistent with a “simple” cosmological constant Λ. Thus although Λ need not actually be a constant, it appears that it probably is..

Physically, Λ is an energy density associated with empty space, sometimes referred to as “vacuum energy” (or, as we will see, “dark energy”). Our understanding of cosmology requires it to exist, but at present we do not have a good explanation for its physical origin; indeed most attempts to explain Λ from known physics fail by very large factors. This is one of the most important unsolved problems in modern physics.
